intro: In meetings you learnt to clarify and sum up, and in the hedging lesson you learnt to soften what you say. Today you'll put both to work in a **negotiation**: making and answering proposals, bargaining with **if** and **provided that**, saying no clearly but politely, and closing the deal so everyone agrees on the same terms. Warm-up: think of the last time you agreed a price, at a market or at work. Who gave way first?
teachingNotes: This functional lesson builds on b2-meetings (clarifying and checking: Sorry, could you clarify what you mean by …?, Just to be clear, …?, So what you're saying is …?; summarising: So, to sum up, …, Let me recap the action points) and c1-hedging (softening a claim, one hedge is enough, would / could / might as softeners), plus the first and second conditionals from B1 (no will after if; second conditional for imagined or unlikely situations) and the business vocabulary of b2-vocab-work-business. Recap those in a line; don't re-teach them. New here: making and responding to proposals, conditional bargaining and trading concessions, saying no diplomatically, handling deadlock, and closing a deal. Contexts: a coffee exporter in Medan (Sari) and a buyer in Melbourne (Mark), a software company in Jakarta (Dimas) and a Jakarta bank (Bu Ani in procurement), a hotel in Ubud, Bali and a tour operator; prices in USD or rupiah.

Proposals: We'd like to propose … (formal, + noun), How would you feel about …? (+ noun or -ing), What if we …? (+ past form = more tentative, like the second conditional: What if we shared the shipping costs?; What if we share …? is also fine). Responses: That sounds reasonable in principle (agree with the idea, details still open), I'm afraid that wouldn't work for us, because … (always give the reason), Could you be a bit more flexible on …?. Likely errors to correct: 'Can discount?' / 'Bisa kurang?' translated → Could you be a bit more flexible on the price?; 'Your price is too expensive' → The price is a bit higher than we expected (a price is high, a product is expensive); 'We propose you a discount' → We'd like to offer you a discount / We'd like to propose a discount (propose takes the thing, not the person); 'in principal' → in principle (same sound, different word).

Bargaining: an offer with a condition. Real offer, first conditional: If you can increase the order to 5,000 units, we could offer a 7% discount / If you pay within 14 days, we'll cover the shipping. Tentative idea, second conditional: If you signed for three years, we could lower the monthly fee. 'If you can …, we could …' is normal in negotiation (could = softer): accept it, and accept would / could / can in the result. 'only if' words: provided that / providing (asalkan, formal), as long as (asalkan, a little less formal), on condition that (very formal). We'd be prepared to … / We'd be willing to … (kami bersedia). Softening from c1-hedging: That might be difficult; We were hoping for something closer to … (past continuous = softer, the hope is still now). Strategy: never give a concession (something you give up) without getting something back. Likely errors: 'If you will order 5,000 units, we give you discount 7%' → If you order 5,000 units, we'll give you a 7% discount (no will after if; a + number + discount, while Indonesian says diskon 7%); 'provide that' → provided that; 'as soon as' (= segera setelah, time) used for 'as long as' (= asalkan, condition); giving away a discount with no condition.

Saying no and deadlock, with culture: many Indonesians avoid a direct tidak and say nanti kami pertimbangkan, kami usahakan or insyaallah when they mean no; many foreign partners hear 'maybe yes', wait, and later feel misled. Teach a diplomatic but clear no: soft start (I'm afraid / Unfortunately) + the no + the reason + an alternative if there is one (but we could … instead). 'We'll think about it' is fine only if you really will. Haggling at a pasar starts far apart and meets in the middle; in formal B2B talks with foreign partners an extreme first offer can damage trust: start realistic, give a reason for every number, move in small conditional steps. Relationship first is valued in English-speaking business too (small talk, trust), but terms must be explicit and confirmed in writing. Present this respectfully, as a habit to adapt, not as a criticism. Deadlock (jalan buntu): Let's look at it from a different angle; Is there any room for manoeuvre on …? (manoeuvre British, maneuver American); Let's take a short break.

Closing: summarise every term (what and how much, when, how you pay, any condition): So, just to confirm: delivery by 15 March, payment within 30 days, 7% discount. Is that right?; check agreement (Is that right? / Have I missed anything?); next steps with who and when (We'll send the contract by Friday); end on a positive note (It's been a pleasure doing business with you; We're looking forward to working with you). A summary that leaves out the price or the payment terms is incomplete. Much of negotiation English is style: accept reasonable alternatives (willing / prepared / happy; Just to clarify / Just to recap for confirm) and only mark clear cases wrong: will in the if-part, as soon as for as long as, a vague or blunt no, a concession with no condition, an incomplete summary.

Limits: A0–B2 grammar plus the chain. No inversion (Should you …, Were we to …), subjunctive (we insist that he pay), cleft sentences ('What we could do is …') or impersonal passives in examples; a learner who meets 'Should you have any questions' gets it as a phrase to remember. Don't teach contract law, Incoterms (FOB, CIF) or idioms like lowball / dealbreaker beyond a mention. Correct one thing at a time, usually 'discount 7%', will after if, 'too expensive price' or the indirect 'we'll think about it' no.

keyPoints.title: Make and respond to proposals
keyPoints.explanation: Make a proposal with We'd like to propose … (formal), How would you feel about …? (+ noun or -ing) or What if we …? (What if we shared … sounds more tentative). Respond with That sounds reasonable in principle (yes to the idea, details still open), I'm afraid that wouldn't work for us, because … (a clear no with a reason) or Could you be a bit more flexible on …?. Say 'the price is high', not 'the price is too expensive'.

examples.en: We'd like to propose a two-year contract with a fixed monthly fee.
examples.id: Kami ingin mengusulkan kontrak dua tahun dengan biaya bulanan tetap.

examples.en: How would you feel about paying 30% in advance?
examples.id: Bagaimana pendapat Anda kalau 30% dibayar di muka?

examples.en: I'm afraid that wouldn't work for us, because our budget is fixed until January.
examples.id: Maaf, itu tidak bisa kami terima, karena anggaran kami sudah tetap sampai Januari.

id.title: Membuat dan menanggapi usulan
id.explanation: Buat usulan dengan We'd like to propose … (formal), How would you feel about …? (+ kata benda atau bentuk -ing) atau What if we …? (What if we shared … terdengar lebih hati-hati). Tanggapi dengan That sounds reasonable in principle (setuju dengan idenya, detailnya masih terbuka), I'm afraid that wouldn't work for us, because … (penolakan yang jelas, dengan alasan) atau Could you be a bit more flexible on …? (bisakah Anda sedikit lebih fleksibel soal …?). Katakan 'the price is high', bukan 'the price is too expensive'.

keyPoints.title: Bargain with conditions, and never give without getting
keyPoints.explanation: Make offers with a condition: If you can increase the order to 5,000 units, we could offer a 7% discount (no will after if). For a more tentative idea, use the second conditional: If you signed for three years, we could lower the fee. Other 'only if' words: provided that / as long as (asalkan); not as soon as. We'd be prepared to … / We'd be willing to … = kami bersedia. Soften: That might be difficult; We were hoping for something closer to …. Every concession comes with an 'if'. To get out of deadlock: Is there any room for manoeuvre on …? / Let's take a short break.

examples.en: If you pay within 14 days, we'll cover the shipping to Melbourne.
examples.id: Kalau Anda membayar dalam 14 hari, kami yang menanggung ongkos kirim ke Melbourne.

examples.en: We'd be willing to hold this rate until December, as long as you book 30 rooms a night.
examples.id: Kami bersedia mempertahankan tarif ini sampai Desember, asalkan Anda memesan 30 kamar per malam.

examples.en: We were hoping for something closer to $6.80 per kilo.
examples.id: Kami berharap angkanya lebih dekat ke 6,80 dolar per kilo.

id.title: Menawar dengan syarat, dan jangan memberi tanpa mendapat
id.explanation: Buat tawaran dengan syarat: If you can increase the order to 5,000 units, we could offer a 7% discount (tidak ada will setelah if). Untuk ide yang lebih hati-hati, pakai second conditional: If you signed for three years, we could lower the fee. Kata lain untuk 'hanya kalau': provided that / as long as (asalkan); bukan as soon as. We'd be prepared to … / We'd be willing to … = kami bersedia. Perhalus: That might be difficult; We were hoping for something closer to …. Setiap konsesi (hal yang kamu relakan) selalu disertai 'if'. Untuk keluar dari jalan buntu: Is there any room for manoeuvre on …? / Let's take a short break.

keyPoints.title: Close the deal and confirm the terms
keyPoints.explanation: Before you finish, summarise every term (what and how much, when, how you pay, any condition) and check: So, just to confirm: delivery by 15 March, payment within 30 days, 7% discount. Is that right?. Then give the next steps with who and when (We'll send the contract by Friday) and end on a positive note (It's been a pleasure doing business with you). Confirm it in writing the same day.

examples.en: So, just to confirm: 20 tonnes at $6.50 per kilo, delivery by 15 March and payment within 30 days. Is that right?
examples.id: Jadi, untuk memastikan: 20 ton dengan harga 6,50 dolar per kilo, dikirim paling lambat 15 Maret dan dibayar dalam 30 hari. Betul begitu?

examples.en: We'll send the contract by Friday.
examples.id: Kami akan mengirim kontraknya paling lambat hari Jumat.

examples.en: It's been a pleasure doing business with you.
examples.id: Senang sekali bisa bekerja sama dengan Anda.

id.title: Menutup kesepakatan dan menegaskan ketentuannya
id.explanation: Sebelum selesai, rangkum setiap ketentuan (apa dan berapa, kapan, cara bayar, syarat apa pun) lalu cek: So, just to confirm: delivery by 15 March, payment within 30 days, 7% discount. Is that right?. Lalu sebutkan langkah berikutnya, siapa dan kapan (We'll send the contract by Friday), dan tutup dengan nada positif (It's been a pleasure doing business with you). Tegaskan juga secara tertulis di hari yang sama.

guidedPractice.prompt: Sari, at a coffee exporter in Medan, has a new idea for her buyer in Australia: paying half each for the coffee samples. Complete with one word: What ___ we split the cost of the samples?
The bank likes the general idea of Dimas's proposal, but the timeline still needs to be discussed. Complete with one word: That sounds reasonable in ___, but we need to look at the timeline.
guidedPractice.hint: pada prinsipnya = in … (careful with the spelling: it ends in -ple)

guidedPractice.prompt: Complete the offer with the verb increase in the right form: If you ___ the order to 5,000 units, we can offer a 7% discount.
The buyer offers $5.90 per kilo, but Sari needs about $6.40. Answer softly. Complete with one word: We were ___ for something closer to $6.40.
guidedPractice.hint: berharap = hope; here in the past continuous (were …-ing), which sounds softer.

guidedPractice.prompt: End the call with a clear next step. Complete with one word: We'll ___ you the draft contract by Wednesday.

independentPractice.prompt: The talks are going round in circles and everyone is tired. Suggest a pause. Complete with one word: Let's take a short ___ and come back to this at three.
Open the talks with a formal proposal. Complete with one word: We'd like to ___ a three-year partnership.
The deal is done. End on a positive note. Complete with one word: It's been a ___ doing business with you.

assessment.prompt: Dimas works for a software company in Jakarta. The bank wants a one-year contract, but Dimas would prefer two years. He makes a gentle proposal and asks for the bank's reaction. Complete with one word: How would you ___ about a two-year contract instead?
assessment.rubric: Correct: feel (How would you feel about …? = bagaimana pendapat Anda soal …?). 'think' = 40 ('What would you think about …?' is fine, but 'How would you think about' isn't natural). 'feeling' = 40 (after would, use the base form). 'say' = 30. 'agree' = 20 (it would need 'with' or 'to', and it isn't a question about their reaction).

assessment.prompt: A hotel in Ubud, Bali and a tour operator are discussing a contract. After an hour, they are stuck on the cancellation policy: the tour operator wants free cancellation up to 7 days before arrival, the hotel wants 30 days. Ask politely whether the other side can change its position at all. Complete with one word: Is there any ___ for manoeuvre on the cancellation period?
assessment.rubric: Correct: room (room for manoeuvre = ruang untuk bergeser, kelonggaran). 'space' = 50 (understood, but the fixed phrase is room for manoeuvre). 'flexibility' = 50 (a good word, but 'flexibility for manoeuvre' isn't the phrase: say 'Is there any flexibility on …?'). 'chance' or 'possibility' = 30. 'rooms' = 60 (room here is uncountable: no -s).

assessment.prompt: The bank asks Dimas's company for 60 days to pay instead of 30. Dimas can accept, but only if the bank signs for two years. Complete with one word: We'd be ___ to extend the payment period to 60 days if you sign a two-year contract.
assessment.rubric: Correct: prepared or willing (We'd be prepared / willing to … = kami bersedia). 'happy', 'able', 'ready', 'glad' = 100. 'prepare' = 50 (after be, you need the adjective prepared). 'agree' = 30 ('We'd be agree' copies the Indonesian 'kami setuju': say 'We'd agree to …' without be). 'can' = 0.

assessment.prompt: The hotel in Bali offers the tour operator free airport transfers, but only for groups that stay three nights or more. Complete with one word: We can include free airport transfers, ___ that your groups stay at least three nights.
assessment.rubric: Correct: provided (provided that = asalkan, dengan syarat). 'providing' = 100 (common in British English). 'on condition' = 100 (two words, but correct: on condition that). 'provide' = 40 (the phrase is provided that). 'given' = 20 (given that = mengingat: it gives a reason, not a condition). 'so' = 0 (so that = supaya: a purpose).

assessment.prompt: Sari, at a coffee exporter in Medan, can keep last year's price for her Australian buyer, but only if the buyer confirms the order this week. Complete with one word: We can keep the price at $6.50 per kilo as ___ as you confirm the order by Friday.
assessment.rubric: Correct: long (as long as = asalkan, a condition). 'soon' = 30 (as soon as = segera setelah: it's about time, so the price would depend on nothing). 'far' = 0. 'well' = 0.

assessment.prompt: Read the Australian buyer's message to Sari: 'We'd be happy to pay 50% in advance, as long as you can ship the coffee by 1 March.' What does Sari's company have to do to get the advance payment? Answer in English with a short phrase, like this example: send the samples by 5 May.
acceptableAnswers: ship the coffee by the 1st of march
they have to ship the coffee by 1 march
we have to ship the coffee by 1 march
assessment.rubric: Correct: ship the coffee by 1 March (the condition comes after 'as long as'; the advance payment is the result). Any clear form with ship / send and the date = 100. 'deliver the coffee by 1 March' = 70 (ship = send it off; deliver = it arrives, a different promise). Only 'ship the coffee' without the date = 50 (the date is part of the condition). 'pay 50% in advance' = 0 (that's what the buyer offers, not the condition).

assessment.prompt: At the end of the call, Bu Ani, the sales manager of a hotel in Ubud, checks the final terms with the tour operator before she writes the contract. Complete with one word: So, just to ___: 40 rooms a night from June to August, Rp 1,150,000 per room, and free cancellation up to 21 days before arrival. Is that right?
assessment.rubric: Correct: confirm (So, just to confirm: … Is that right? = jadi, untuk memastikan …). 'check', 'clarify', 'recap', 'summarise' / 'summarize' and 'be clear' = 100. 'confirmation' = 50 (after to, use the verb). 'conclude' = 30 (it means to finish or to decide, not to check the terms). 'agree' = 30.

blocks.text:
Quick recap: in meetings you learnt to clarify and check (*Just to be clear, …?*, *So what you're saying is …?*) and to sum up; in the hedging lesson you learnt to soften a claim with one hedge. A **negotiation** (negosiasi, perundingan) needs both, plus a few new tools.

**Making a proposal** (usulan):
- ***We'd like to propose …*** + noun (formal, often at the start): *We'd like to propose a two-year contract.*
- ***How would you feel about …?*** + noun or -ing (bagaimana pendapat Anda soal …?): *How would you feel about paying 30% in advance?*
- ***What if we …?*** (bagaimana kalau kita …?): *What if we shared the shipping costs?* The past form *shared* doesn't mean the past here: like the second conditional, it makes the idea sound more tentative (lebih hati-hati, 'cuma ide'). *What if we share …?* is fine too.

**Responding** (menanggapi):
- yes to the idea, details still open: ***That sounds reasonable in principle.*** (pada prinsipnya masuk akal)
- no, with a reason: ***I'm afraid that wouldn't work for us, because …***
- asking them to move: ***Could you be a bit more flexible on …?*** (the price, the delivery date, the payment terms)

Why *would* and *could*? They make your words sound like something to discuss, not a demand. *That won't work* sounds final; *That wouldn't work for us* is just as clear, but polite.

id.text:
Ulasan singkat: di pelajaran rapat kamu belajar mengklarifikasi dan mengecek (*Just to be clear, …?*, *So what you're saying is …?*) dan merangkum; di pelajaran hedging kamu belajar melunakkan klaim dengan satu pelunak. **Negosiasi** (perundingan) butuh keduanya, ditambah beberapa alat baru.

**Membuat usulan:**
- ***We'd like to propose …*** + kata benda (formal, sering di awal): *We'd like to propose a two-year contract.* (kami ingin mengusulkan kontrak dua tahun)
- ***How would you feel about …?*** + kata benda atau bentuk -ing (bagaimana pendapat Anda soal …?): *How would you feel about paying 30% in advance?*
- ***What if we …?*** (bagaimana kalau kita …?): *What if we shared the shipping costs?* Bentuk lampau *shared* di sini bukan berarti masa lalu: seperti second conditional, bentuk ini membuat idenya terdengar lebih hati-hati ('cuma ide'). *What if we share …?* juga boleh.

**Menanggapi:**
- setuju dengan idenya, detailnya masih terbuka: ***That sounds reasonable in principle.*** (pada prinsipnya masuk akal)
- menolak, dengan alasan: ***I'm afraid that wouldn't work for us, because …*** (maaf, itu tidak bisa kami terima, karena …)
- meminta mereka bergeser: ***Could you be a bit more flexible on …?*** (bisakah Anda sedikit lebih fleksibel soal harga, tanggal kirim, cara bayar?)

Kenapa *would* dan *could*? Kata-kata ini membuat ucapanmu terdengar seperti bahan diskusi, bukan tuntutan. *That won't work* terdengar final; *That wouldn't work for us* sama jelasnya, tapi sopan.

blocks.text:
Four Indonesian traps:
- **'Bisa kurang?' is not `Can discount?` ✗.** At a pasar that's normal, but in a business meeting say **Could you be a bit more flexible on the price?**
- **`Your price is too expensive` ✗.** In English a *product* is expensive, but a *price* is **high**: **The price is a bit higher than we expected.** (Also softer: it talks about the price, not about *your* price.)
- **`We propose you a discount` ✗.** *propose* takes the thing, not the person: **We'd like to propose a discount** or **We'd like to offer you a discount.**
- **principle ≠ principal.** They sound the same, but **in principle** = pada prinsipnya; *principal* = kepala sekolah, or the main amount of a loan.

id.text:
Empat jebakan dari bahasa Indonesia:
- **'Bisa kurang?' bukan `Can discount?` ✗.** Di pasar itu wajar, tapi di rapat bisnis katakan **Could you be a bit more flexible on the price?**
- **`Your price is too expensive` ✗.** Dalam bahasa Inggris, *barang* bisa expensive, tapi *harga* itu **high**: **The price is a bit higher than we expected.** (Juga lebih halus: yang dibahas harganya, bukan harga *Anda*.)
- **`We propose you a discount` ✗.** *propose* diikuti bendanya, bukan orangnya: **We'd like to propose a discount** atau **We'd like to offer you a discount.**
- **principle ≠ principal.** Bunyinya sama, tapi **in principle** = pada prinsipnya; *principal* = kepala sekolah, atau pokok pinjaman.

blocks.prompt: The bank's IT team suggests starting the project in March, not January. Dimas likes the idea, but the price for the extra months still has to be agreed. Which reply fits best?
options: That sounds reasonable in principle, but we'd need to agree on the price first.
blocks.explain: **That sounds reasonable in principle** says yes to the idea while keeping the details (here the price) open. *Deal!* closes everything too early, before the price is agreed, and an idea isn't *expensive*: it's the price that's high.

id.prompt: Tim IT bank mengusulkan proyeknya dimulai bulan Maret, bukan Januari. Dimas suka idenya, tapi harga untuk bulan-bulan tambahan belum disepakati. Tanggapan mana yang paling pas?
id.explain: **That sounds reasonable in principle** berarti setuju dengan idenya sambil membiarkan detailnya (di sini harganya) tetap terbuka. *Deal!* menutup semuanya terlalu cepat, sebelum harganya disepakati, dan sebuah ide tidak bisa *expensive*: yang tinggi itu harganya.

material.title: Bargaining with conditions: if, provided that, as long as

blocks.text:
In a negotiation you rarely give a plain *yes*. You say **yes, if …**: an offer with a **condition** (syarat). It's the conditional you already know:
- **A real offer** (first conditional, if + present): ***If you can increase the order to 5,000 units, we could offer a 7% discount.*** / *If you pay within 14 days, we'll cover the shipping.* As always, no *will* after *if*.
- **A tentative idea** (second conditional, if + past): ***If you signed for three years, we could lower the monthly fee.*** The past form says 'we're only exploring this'.

*If you can …, we could …* mixes the two, and that's normal in negotiations: *could* in the result just sounds softer than *can*.

**Other ways to say 'only if':**
- ***provided that*** / ***providing*** (asalkan, dengan syarat): formal.
- ***as long as*** (asalkan): a little less formal. Not *as soon as* (= segera setelah, about time).
- ***on condition that*** (dengan syarat): very formal, common in contracts.

**Saying what you could give:** ***We'd be prepared to …*** / ***We'd be willing to …*** (kami bersedia …): *We'd be willing to hold this rate until December, as long as you book 30 rooms a night.*

**Softening** (from the hedging lesson): ***That might be difficult.*** / ***We were hoping for something closer to …*** The past continuous (*were hoping*) doesn't mean the hope is over: it just sounds less pushy than *We hope for …*.

id.text:
Dalam negosiasi kamu jarang menjawab *yes* begitu saja. Kamu bilang **yes, if …**: tawaran dengan **syarat**. Ini conditional yang sudah kamu kenal:
- **Tawaran nyata** (first conditional, if + present): ***If you can increase the order to 5,000 units, we could offer a 7% discount.*** (kalau Anda bisa menaikkan pesanan jadi 5.000 unit, kami bisa memberi diskon 7%) / *If you pay within 14 days, we'll cover the shipping.* Seperti biasa, tidak ada *will* setelah *if*.
- **Ide yang masih dijajaki** (second conditional, if + past): ***If you signed for three years, we could lower the monthly fee.*** Bentuk lampaunya berarti 'kami baru menjajaki ini'.

*If you can …, we could …* mencampur keduanya, dan itu wajar dalam negosiasi: *could* di bagian hasil hanya terdengar lebih halus daripada *can*.

**Cara lain untuk bilang 'hanya kalau':**
- ***provided that*** / ***providing*** (asalkan, dengan syarat): formal.
- ***as long as*** (asalkan): sedikit kurang formal. Bukan *as soon as* (= segera setelah, soal waktu).
- ***on condition that*** (dengan syarat): sangat formal, sering di kontrak.

**Menyebut apa yang bisa kamu berikan:** ***We'd be prepared to …*** / ***We'd be willing to …*** (kami bersedia …): *We'd be willing to hold this rate until December, as long as you book 30 rooms a night.*

**Memperhalus** (dari pelajaran hedging): ***That might be difficult.*** (itu mungkin sulit) / ***We were hoping for something closer to …*** (kami berharap angkanya lebih dekat ke …). Past continuous (*were hoping*) bukan berarti harapannya sudah lewat: bentuk ini hanya terdengar kurang memaksa daripada *We hope for …*.

id.note: were hoping: lebih halus, bukan berarti sudah selesai

blocks.text:
**Never give something without getting something.** A **concession** (konsesi: something you give up) should always come with an *if*: *We could go to 6%, if you …*. If you just say *OK, 10% off*, the other side learns your first price wasn't real, and asks for more.

Indonesian traps:
- `If you will order 5,000 units, we give you discount 7%.` ✗ → **If you order 5,000 units, we'll give you a 7% discount.** Three fixes: no *will* after *if*; *will* or *can* in the result; and **a 7% discount** (a + the number before *discount*; Indonesian *diskon 7%* puts it after).
- `provide that` ✗ → **provided that** / **providing**.
- **as long as ≠ as soon as.** *as long as* = asalkan; *as soon as* = segera setelah.

**Pasar or boardroom?** At a pasar, haggling starts far apart: the seller asks double, you offer half, and you meet in the middle (*Kurang ya, Bu?*). In formal talks with foreign partners, a first offer that's extremely low can damage trust. Start realistic, give a reason for every number, and move in small steps, each with a condition.

id.text:
**Jangan pernah memberi tanpa mendapat sesuatu.** **Konsesi** (hal yang kamu relakan) selalu disertai *if*: *We could go to 6%, if you …*. Kalau kamu langsung bilang *OK, 10% off*, pihak lain jadi tahu harga awalmu tidak serius, lalu minta lebih.

Jebakan dari bahasa Indonesia:
- `If you will order 5,000 units, we give you discount 7%.` ✗ → **If you order 5,000 units, we'll give you a 7% discount.** Tiga perbaikan: tidak ada *will* setelah *if*; *will* atau *can* di bagian hasil; dan **a 7% discount** (a + angkanya sebelum *discount*; bahasa Indonesia *diskon 7%* menaruhnya di belakang).
- `provide that` ✗ → **provided that** / **providing**.
- **as long as ≠ as soon as.** *as long as* = asalkan; *as soon as* = segera setelah.

**Pasar atau ruang rapat?** Di pasar, tawar-menawar dimulai dari jarak yang jauh: penjual minta dua kali lipat, kamu menawar setengah, lalu bertemu di tengah (*Kurang ya, Bu?*). Dalam perundingan formal dengan mitra asing, tawaran pertama yang terlalu rendah bisa merusak kepercayaan. Mulailah dengan angka yang realistis, beri alasan untuk setiap angka, dan bergeser sedikit demi sedikit, masing-masing dengan syarat.

blocks.prompt: Sari wants $6.60 per kilo for her coffee. The Australian buyer offers $5.90. Sari won't accept $5.90, but she wants to keep the talks friendly. Which reply is firm but polite?
options: We were hoping for something closer to $6.50.
blocks.explain: **We were hoping for something closer to …** says no to $5.90 and names a new number, softly. *Your price is too cheap!* sounds like an attack (and a price is *low*, not *cheap*), and *OK, $5.90 is fine* gives everything away without getting anything back.

id.prompt: Sari ingin harga 6,60 dolar per kilo untuk kopinya. Pembeli dari Australia menawar 5,90 dolar. Sari tidak mau menerima 5,90 dolar, tapi ingin perundingannya tetap bersahabat. Jawaban mana yang tegas tapi sopan?
id.explain: **We were hoping for something closer to …** menolak 5,90 dolar dan menyebut angka baru, dengan halus. *Your price is too cheap!* terdengar menyerang (dan harga itu *low*, bukan *cheap*), sedangkan *OK, $5.90 is fine* menyerahkan semuanya tanpa mendapat apa-apa.

id.title: Menawar dengan syarat: if, provided that, as long as

material.title: Saying no clearly, and getting out of deadlock

blocks.text:
**The 'maybe' trap.** In Indonesia, a direct *tidak* can feel rude, so we often say *nanti kami pertimbangkan*, *kami usahakan* or *insyaallah* when we really mean no. Many foreign partners hear these as **'maybe yes'**: they wait, plan around it, and later feel misled. In English, a diplomatic no is still a **clear** no. Use up to four parts:
1. a soft start: ***I'm afraid …*** / ***Unfortunately, …***
2. the no: ***… that wouldn't work for us*** / ***we're not in a position to …*** (kami tidak bisa …)
3. the reason: ***… because …***
4. an alternative, if you have one: ***But we could … instead.***

*We'll think about it* is fine only when you really will think about it.

**Deadlock** (jalan buntu): both sides are stuck. Ways out:
- ***Let's look at it from a different angle.*** (mari kita lihat dari sudut pandang lain)
- ***Is there any room for manoeuvre on …?*** (ada kelonggaran soal …?) *manoeuvre* is the British spelling, *maneuver* the American; both are said like 'me-NU-ver'.
- ***Let's take a short break.*** A break lets both sides cool down and check with their boss.
- ***What matters most to you here?*** Find out what the other side really needs: maybe it's the date, not the price.

id.text:
**Jebakan 'mungkin'.** Di Indonesia, *tidak* yang langsung bisa terasa kasar, jadi kita sering bilang *nanti kami pertimbangkan*, *kami usahakan* atau *insyaallah* padahal maksudnya tidak. Banyak mitra asing mendengarnya sebagai **'mungkin ya'**: mereka menunggu, membuat rencana berdasarkan itu, lalu merasa dibohongi. Dalam bahasa Inggris, penolakan yang diplomatis tetap penolakan yang **jelas**. Pakai sampai empat bagian:
1. pembuka yang halus: ***I'm afraid …*** / ***Unfortunately, …*** (sayangnya …)
2. penolakannya: ***… that wouldn't work for us*** / ***we're not in a position to …*** (kami tidak bisa …)
3. alasannya: ***… because …***
4. alternatif, kalau ada: ***But we could … instead.*** (tapi kami bisa … sebagai gantinya)

*We'll think about it* hanya boleh dipakai kalau kamu memang akan memikirkannya.

**Deadlock** (jalan buntu): kedua pihak macet. Cara keluarnya:
- ***Let's look at it from a different angle.*** (mari kita lihat dari sudut pandang lain)
- ***Is there any room for manoeuvre on …?*** (ada kelonggaran soal …?) *manoeuvre* ejaan British, *maneuver* ejaan Amerika; keduanya dibaca kira-kira 'me-NU-ver'.
- ***Let's take a short break.*** (kita istirahat sebentar) Jeda memberi kedua pihak waktu untuk tenang dan bertanya ke atasannya.
- ***What matters most to you here?*** (apa yang paling penting bagi Anda?) Cari tahu apa yang benar-benar dibutuhkan pihak lain: mungkin tanggalnya, bukan harganya.

rows.en: I'm afraid that wouldn't work for us, because our costs have gone up this year.
rows.id: Maaf, itu tidak bisa kami terima, karena biaya kami naik tahun ini.

rows.en: Unfortunately, we're not in a position to lower the price any further.
rows.id: Sayangnya, kami tidak bisa menurunkan harganya lagi.

rows.en: We can't include free dinners, but we could offer free breakfast instead.
rows.id: Kami tidak bisa memberi makan malam gratis, tapi kami bisa memberi sarapan gratis sebagai gantinya.

rows.en: Let's look at it from a different angle: what matters most to you, the price or the delivery date?
rows.id: Mari kita lihat dari sudut pandang lain: mana yang paling penting bagi Anda, harganya atau tanggal pengirimannya?

rows.en: Is there any room for manoeuvre on the payment terms?
rows.id: Apakah ada kelonggaran soal ketentuan pembayarannya?

rows.en: Shall we take a short break? We can continue after lunch.
rows.id: Bagaimana kalau kita istirahat sebentar? Kita bisa lanjut setelah makan siang.

blocks.text:
**Relationship first, terms in writing.** In many Indonesian companies, the relationship comes first: getting to know each other, sharing a meal, building trust. That's valued in English-speaking business too: a little small talk and a friendly tone help. But a good relationship doesn't replace clear terms. Being clear about a no isn't rude; to most international partners it shows respect and builds trust.

And from the other side: if a partner says something vague like *That's an interesting idea*, check it, as you learnt in meetings: **Just to be clear, is that a no for now?**

id.text:
**Hubungan dulu, ketentuan tertulis.** Di banyak perusahaan Indonesia, hubungan diutamakan: saling kenal, makan bersama, membangun kepercayaan. Itu juga dihargai dalam bisnis berbahasa Inggris: sedikit basa-basi dan nada yang ramah membantu. Tapi hubungan yang baik tidak menggantikan ketentuan yang jelas. Menolak dengan jelas itu tidak kasar; bagi kebanyakan mitra internasional, itu tanda hormat dan membangun kepercayaan.

Dan dari sisi sebaliknya: kalau mitramu mengatakan sesuatu yang samar seperti *That's an interesting idea*, cek dulu, seperti yang kamu pelajari di pelajaran rapat: **Just to be clear, is that a no for now?** (biar jelas, untuk sekarang jawabannya tidak, ya?)

blocks.prompt: The talks between Dimas and the bank have been stuck on the price for an hour. Everyone is tired, and Dimas needs to call his CEO before he can offer anything new. What's the best thing to say?
options: Let's take a short break and continue in twenty minutes.
blocks.explain: A **short break** gets everyone out of the deadlock and gives Dimas time to call his CEO. Accepting the price gives everything away without getting anything back, and walking out ends the talks.

id.prompt: Perundingan antara Dimas dan pihak bank sudah macet soal harga selama satu jam. Semua orang lelah, dan Dimas perlu menelepon CEO-nya sebelum bisa menawarkan sesuatu yang baru. Apa yang paling baik untuk dikatakan?
id.explain: **Istirahat sebentar** membawa semua orang keluar dari jalan buntu dan memberi Dimas waktu untuk menelepon CEO-nya. Menerima harganya berarti menyerahkan semuanya tanpa mendapat apa-apa, dan pergi begitu saja mengakhiri perundingan.

id.title: Menolak dengan jelas, dan keluar dari jalan buntu

material.title: Closing the deal: a whole negotiation

blocks.text:
When you reach agreement, don't just say *Deal!* and leave. Close in four moves:
1. **Summarise the terms** (ketentuan): every number, date and condition. ***So, just to confirm: …*** / ***Let me just run through what we've agreed.***
2. **Check agreement:** ***Is that right?*** / ***Have I missed anything?***
3. **Next steps**, who does what and by when: ***We'll send the contract by Friday.*** / ***Our legal team will review it next week.***
4. **End on a positive note:** ***I think this is a good deal for both of us.*** / ***It's been a pleasure doing business with you.*** / ***We're looking forward to working with you.***

A **complete** summary has: **what and how much** (product, quantity, price), **when** (delivery), **how you pay** (payment terms) and **any conditions** (a discount, an *if*). The piece you leave out is the piece people argue about later.

Here's a whole negotiation between Sari, at a coffee exporter in Medan, and Mark, a buyer in Melbourne. Find the proposal, the no, the conditional offer and the summary.

id.text:
Saat sudah sepakat, jangan hanya bilang *Deal!* lalu pergi. Tutup dengan empat langkah:
1. **Rangkum ketentuannya:** setiap angka, tanggal dan syarat. ***So, just to confirm: …*** (jadi, untuk memastikan: …) / ***Let me just run through what we've agreed.*** (saya ulang sebentar apa yang sudah kita sepakati)
2. **Cek persetujuannya:** ***Is that right?*** (betul begitu?) / ***Have I missed anything?*** (ada yang terlewat?)
3. **Langkah berikutnya**, siapa melakukan apa dan kapan: ***We'll send the contract by Friday.*** / ***Our legal team will review it next week.***
4. **Tutup dengan nada positif:** ***I think this is a good deal for both of us.*** / ***It's been a pleasure doing business with you.*** / ***We're looking forward to working with you.***

Rangkuman yang **lengkap** berisi: **apa dan berapa** (produk, jumlah, harga), **kapan** (pengiriman), **cara bayar** (ketentuan pembayaran) dan **syarat apa pun** (diskon, sebuah *if*). Bagian yang kamu lewatkan adalah bagian yang nanti diperdebatkan.

Ini negosiasi lengkap antara Sari, dari eksportir kopi di Medan, dan Mark, pembeli di Melbourne. Temukan usulan, penolakan, tawaran bersyarat dan rangkumannya.

rows.en: Mark: We'd like to propose 20 tonnes at $6.20 per kilo.
rows.id: Mark: Kami ingin mengusulkan 20 ton dengan harga 6,20 dolar per kilo.

rows.en: Sari: I'm afraid that wouldn't work for us. Our costs have gone up this year, so we were hoping for something closer to $6.80.
rows.id: Sari: Maaf, itu tidak bisa kami terima. Biaya kami naik tahun ini, jadi kami berharap angkanya lebih dekat ke 6,80 dolar.

rows.en: Mark: What if we met in the middle? If you can deliver by 15 March, we could pay $6.50.
rows.id: Mark: Bagaimana kalau kita bertemu di tengah? Kalau Anda bisa mengirim paling lambat 15 Maret, kami bisa membayar 6,50 dolar.

rows.en: Sari: That sounds reasonable in principle. We'd be prepared to accept $6.50, as long as you pay within 30 days.
rows.id: Sari: Pada prinsipnya itu masuk akal. Kami bersedia menerima 6,50 dolar, asalkan Anda membayar dalam 30 hari.

rows.en: Mark: That works for us.
rows.id: Mark: Itu cocok untuk kami.

rows.en: Sari: So, just to confirm: 20 tonnes at $6.50 per kilo, delivery by 15 March and payment within 30 days. Is that right?
rows.id: Sari: Jadi, untuk memastikan: 20 ton dengan harga 6,50 dolar per kilo, dikirim paling lambat 15 Maret dan dibayar dalam 30 hari. Betul begitu?

rows.en: Mark: Yes, that's right. We'll send the contract by Friday.
rows.id: Mark: Ya, betul. Kami akan mengirim kontraknya paling lambat hari Jumat.

rows.en: Sari: Great. It's been a pleasure doing business with you.
rows.id: Sari: Bagus. Senang sekali bisa bekerja sama dengan Anda.

blocks.text:
**Confirm it in writing, the same day.** A handshake or a friendly call can feel like enough, especially when the relationship is good. International partners still expect the terms in an email soon after: *Following our call today, I'm writing to confirm the terms we agreed: …* (the formal email style you already know). It protects both sides and isn't a sign of distrust.

*Deal!* is fine between people who know each other well; *Agreed.* or *That works for us.* sound more professional.

id.text:
**Tegaskan secara tertulis, di hari yang sama.** Jabat tangan atau telepon yang ramah bisa terasa cukup, apalagi kalau hubungannya baik. Mitra internasional tetap mengharapkan ketentuannya dikirim lewat email tidak lama kemudian: *Following our call today, I'm writing to confirm the terms we agreed: …* (gaya email formal yang sudah kamu kenal). Ini melindungi kedua pihak dan bukan tanda tidak percaya.

*Deal!* boleh di antara orang yang sudah saling kenal baik; *Agreed.* atau *That works for us.* terdengar lebih profesional.

blocks.prompt: The hotel and the tour operator have agreed on all the terms. Which sentence is a clear next step?
options: Maybe we can do something next time.
Our team will send you the draft contract by Thursday.
blocks.explain: A clear next step says **who** (our team), **what** (send the draft contract) and **by when** (by Thursday). *Let's keep in touch* is friendly but gives no action, and *Maybe … next time* sounds as if there's no deal at all.

id.prompt: Pihak hotel dan operator tur sudah menyepakati semua ketentuannya. Kalimat mana yang merupakan langkah berikutnya yang jelas?
id.explain: Langkah berikutnya yang jelas menyebut **siapa** (our team), **apa** (mengirim draf kontrak) dan **kapan** (paling lambat hari Kamis). *Let's keep in touch* ramah, tapi tidak ada tindakannya, dan *Maybe … next time* terdengar seolah-olah tidak ada kesepakatan sama sekali.

resources.title: Work English: Expressions for polite negotiations
resources.note: Polite phrases for negotiating at work, using could, might, should and would to sound less confrontational, and ways to close a deal. Some phrases differ from this lesson (I could look into it, Let's shake on it).

id.note: Ungkapan sopan untuk bernegosiasi di tempat kerja, dengan could, might, should dan would agar tidak terdengar konfrontatif, dan cara menutup kesepakatan. Beberapa ungkapannya berbeda dari pelajaran ini (I could look into it, Let's shake on it).

resources.title: Professional & Business English: Negotiating Vocabulary
resources.note: Vocabulary for talking about negotiations: deadlock, dealbreaker, give-and-take, compromise, middle ground, lowball. It's more about words for describing a negotiation than phrases to use in one, and adds idioms beyond this lesson.

id.note: Kosakata untuk membicarakan negosiasi: deadlock, dealbreaker, give-and-take, compromise, middle ground, lowball. Isinya lebih ke kata-kata untuk menggambarkan negosiasi daripada ungkapan untuk dipakai saat bernegosiasi, dan ada idiom tambahan di luar pelajaran ini.

resources.title: 6 language must-haves to negotiate in English
resources.note: A short article on how negotiations often go in the UK: small talk first, a careful proposal, understatement instead of a direct no, and agreeing the final terms later by email. Useful background for the culture side of this lesson.

id.note: Artikel singkat tentang bagaimana negosiasi sering berjalan di Inggris: basa-basi dulu, usulan yang hati-hati, ungkapan yang diperhalus sebagai ganti penolakan langsung, dan menyepakati ketentuan akhirnya belakangan lewat email. Bagus sebagai latar belakang sisi budaya dalam pelajaran ini.

id.intro: Di pelajaran rapat kamu belajar mengklarifikasi dan merangkum, dan di pelajaran hedging kamu belajar memperhalus ucapan. Hari ini kamu memakai keduanya dalam **negosiasi**: membuat dan menanggapi usulan, menawar dengan **if** dan **provided that**, menolak dengan jelas tapi sopan, lalu menutup kesepakatan supaya semua pihak sepakat pada ketentuan yang sama. Pemanasan: ingat lagi saat terakhir kamu menyepakati harga, di pasar atau di kantor. Siapa yang mengalah duluan?
suggestedQuestions: Bagaimana cara menolak klien tanpa terdengar kasar?
Apa bedanya 'provided that' dan 'as long as'?
Kenapa 'nanti kami pertimbangkan' bisa jadi masalah dalam negosiasi berbahasa Inggris?
Kalau membuat tawaran, aku pakai first conditional atau second conditional?

assessment.ng-1: Dimas bekerja di perusahaan software di Jakarta. Pihak bank ingin kontrak satu tahun, tapi Dimas lebih suka dua tahun. Ia membuat usulan dengan halus dan menanyakan tanggapan pihak bank. Lengkapi dengan satu kata: How would you ___ about a two-year contract instead?
assessment.ng-2: Sebuah hotel di Ubud, Bali dan sebuah operator tur sedang membahas kontrak. Setelah satu jam, mereka macet soal kebijakan pembatalan: operator tur ingin pembatalan gratis sampai 7 hari sebelum kedatangan, hotel ingin 30 hari. Tanyakan dengan sopan apakah pihak lain bisa bergeser sedikit pun. Lengkapi dengan satu kata: Is there any ___ for manoeuvre on the cancellation period?
assessment.ng-3: Pihak bank meminta perusahaan Dimas memberi waktu bayar 60 hari, bukan 30. Dimas bisa menerimanya, tapi hanya kalau bank menandatangani kontrak dua tahun. Lengkapi dengan satu kata: We'd be ___ to extend the payment period to 60 days if you sign a two-year contract.
assessment.ng-4: Hotel di Bali itu menawarkan antar-jemput bandara gratis kepada operator tur, tapi hanya untuk rombongan yang menginap tiga malam atau lebih. Lengkapi dengan satu kata: We can include free airport transfers, ___ that your groups stay at least three nights.
assessment.ng-5: Sari, dari eksportir kopi di Medan, bisa mempertahankan harga tahun lalu untuk pembelinya di Australia, tapi hanya kalau pembeli mengonfirmasi pesanannya minggu ini. Lengkapi dengan satu kata: We can keep the price at $6.50 per kilo as ___ as you confirm the order by Friday.
assessment.ng-6: Baca pesan pembeli dari Australia kepada Sari: 'We'd be happy to pay 50% in advance, as long as you can ship the coffee by 1 March.' Apa yang harus dilakukan perusahaan Sari supaya mendapat pembayaran di muka itu? Jawab dalam bahasa Inggris dengan frasa pendek, seperti contoh ini: send the samples by 5 May.
assessment.ng-7: Di akhir panggilan, Bu Ani, manajer penjualan sebuah hotel di Ubud, mengecek ketentuan akhirnya dengan operator tur sebelum menulis kontrak. Lengkapi dengan satu kata: So, just to ___: 40 rooms a night from June to August, Rp 1,150,000 per room, and free cancellation up to 21 days before arrival. Is that right?
